evaluation.positioning_hook: A widowed ranch mother must protect her dying daughter’s flying horse from a vengeful outsider, even as the miracle forces her to choose between secrecy, faith, and letting go.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional engine is clear and accessible: a sick child, a miraculous animal, and a mother trying to hold the family together. The audience is real, but the fantasy is soft and the premise is more specialty-family than broad four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages with Star the seahorse, then escalates cleanly into Firestar the winged colt and the threat of exposure. The premise is easy to explain in one breath and the miracle is front-loaded.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Karissa has a strong protective-mother spine, and Angelique is vivid as a child whose wonder keeps the story alive. Drew adds warmth, but the supporting cast is functional rather than especially layered.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: A flying horse story anchored in chemo, ranch life, and a mother’s emotional resistance gives the script a distinctive lane. The angelic reveal at the end is bold, though the surrounding storytelling stays fairly traditional.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script has a steady forward drive through discovery, secrecy, exposure, and threat, with Thompson giving the back half a clear antagonist. Some middle passages repeat the same emotional argument about belief versus skepticism rather than turning the plot.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of a terminally ill child, a miraculous animal, and a rural family under pressure feels fresh and immediately legible. It’s not just a novelty image; the horse becomes the emotional mechanism that changes the mother.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The ranch/stable world has enough texture to feel lived-in, with horse care, guests, and the local office giving it shape. But the world mostly serves the miracle plot rather than generating a deeper social system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a clear faith-tinged, small-town wonder tone that keeps the fantasy grounded in domestic emotion. The final angelic reveal pushes it into a more mythic register without losing the family-drama core.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material around memory, faith, loss, and what Karissa has forgotten about Star. The script gestures toward that depth, but it stays mostly on the surface of the miracle and the immediate family crisis.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Karissa/Angelique/Drew gives the story a workable family triangle, and Ted/Ed/Thompson add pressure and contrast. Still, the relationships are more support structure than engine; the movie lives primarily on Karissa and Angelique.

lead_characters.name: Karissa Boone
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, middle-aged, white, New England-rooted ranch owner/mother.
lead_characters.hook: A hard-working, emotionally guarded ranch mother who has spent years managing her daughter’s illness and her own disappointment, Karissa is the story’s skeptical center. She starts as the practical adult who wants reality, control, and privacy, then slowly becomes the woman who has to accept that wonder may be the only thing keeping her family alive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Frances McDormand in a more tender register or Laura Linney in a family-centered prestige drama — a role built on contained grief, dry resistance, and a late emotional opening that can reframe the whole film.

lead_characters.name: Angelique Boone
lead_characters.demographics: Girl, early teens, white, cancer patient.
lead_characters.hook: Angelique is the child heart of the movie: observant, brave, funny, and spiritually open in a way her mother isn’t. She’s bedridden one minute and emotionally commanding the next, and her bond with Firestar gives the story its innocence and ache.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young performer the emotional authority of Abigail Breslin in Little Miss Sunshine — a child part with wit, fragility, and the ability to carry the audience’s heart.

lead_characters.name: Drew Boone
lead_characters.demographics: Man, older adult, white, ranch hand/father figure.
lead_characters.hook: Drew is the calm, weathered counterweight to Karissa’s anxiety, a man who speaks in parables and keeps the family emotionally afloat. He functions as the movie’s quiet believer, the one who can absorb the impossible without breaking the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the grounded, humane work of Sam Elliott or Richard Jenkins — dry wit, paternal ease, and the ability to make belief feel lived-in rather than preachy.

lead_characters.name: Ted Manning
lead_characters.hook: Ted is the earnest romantic pressure in Karissa’s life, a man whose charm is sincere enough to matter but not so polished that he feels safe. He becomes a bridge between the ordinary world and the miracle, then a test of whether Karissa can trust anyone outside the family circle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid supporting turn in the lane of a Kevin Costner-style romantic ranch figure or a Sam Shepard type — understated charisma, adult longing, and a chance to play decency under pressure.

lead_characters.name: Martin Thompson
lead_characters.demographics: Man, older adult, white, hostile outsider.
lead_characters.hook: Thompson is the story’s human threat: a resentful man from Karissa and Drew’s past who turns obsession into predation. He starts as a creepy familiar face and hardens into the movie’s most overtly dangerous force, the one who wants to monetize the miracle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is juicy antagonist territory in the tradition of a character actor like Stephen Root or John Goodman playing menace with intelligence — a role that lets an actor pivot from sly charm to outright threat.

lead_characters.name: Ed
lead_characters.demographics: Man, young adult, white, stable hand.
lead_characters.hook: Ed is the loose-limbed local who seems harmless until he isn’t, a flirtatious outsider with a secretive streak and a transactional instinct. He gives the movie its most ambiguous human presence, moving between comic relief, voyeurism, and betrayal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a younger character actor a chance to do what Jesse Plemons or Shea Whigham often do well — charm with a shadow underneath, then reveal the cost of that shadow.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Black
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Black is the clinical voice of reality, the man who translates Angelique’s condition into blunt medical terms. He’s not flashy, but he gives the film its institutional pressure and the hard truth that the miracle is not a cure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact prestige-supporting role in the mold of a Tom McCarthy or Richard Schiff part — authority, restraint, and the chance to land one or two devastating lines cleanly.

lead_characters.name: Star
lead_characters.hook: Star is the childhood miracle that quietly establishes the script’s rulebook: this family has seen the impossible before. The seahorse is brief but crucial, because it makes Firestar feel like destiny rather than a random fantasy flourish.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a creature-performance showcase only in the broadest sense, but it gives the production a signature image and a memorable mythic callback that can become trailer-friendly.

casting_characteristics: one child lead carrying emotional weight
creature performance for Firestar and Star

technical.vfx_details: Firestar’s wings, flight, glowing aura, angelic portal, lightning strike, and final angel procession all require visible effects work.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical horse handling, harnessing, and controlled flight illusion setups; possible wind and light effects for the climax.

rights_flags.detail: Kenny Chesney is specifically named in dialogue and a Kenny Chesney song is referenced on the radio.
Garth Brooks is specifically named in dialogue.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as a family-friendly fantasy-drama with streamer and specialty theatrical appeal.

budget.note: Contemporary ranch settings keep the base footprint contained, but Firestar’s flight, the glowing finale, and the angel army push this beyond a simple practical-effects movie.

casting.note: The key lift is Angelique: a child actor has to carry illness, wonder, and emotional authority, while Karissa needs a lead who can play skepticism and maternal vulnerability without overplaying either.

development.note: The script’s emotional spine is clear, but the final angel reveal shifts the movie from rural miracle drama into overt celestial fantasy, which is a tonal and audience-positioning decision buyers will notice.

comp_set.title: The Secret of Roan Inish
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the same family-centered magical realism and child-driven wonder, with a rural setting that treats the supernatural as emotionally real.

comp_set.title: A Dog's Purpose
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it leans on a sentimental animal bond to carry a family audience through grief and healing.

comp_set.title: The Horse Whisperer
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the ranch setting, horse-centered emotional storytelling, and adult family drama wrapped around an animal with symbolic weight.

comp_set.title: The Water Horse
comp_set.why_it_comps: The creature-as-miracle premise and child attachment dynamic are close cousins, especially in how the animal becomes a source of wonder and protection.

audience_target.primary_audience: Families and adult women who respond to emotional, faith-adjacent fantasy with a strong maternal core and a tearful animal bond.
audience_target.demographics: Skews female, 25-54, with family-viewing appeal and a secondary older audience that likes sentimental, inspirational storytelling.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary ranch locations keep the base cost in indie territory, but the flying horse, angelic climax, and creature effects require disciplined VFX planning.

types_of_buyers: faith-adjacent buyer looking for crossover family material
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of heartfelt, accessible fantasy that can play to parents and kids without becoming effects-first spectacle. The ranch setting and illness storyline give it emotional credibility, while the miracle imagery gives it trailer value.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the story resolves as a closed emotional arc around Karissa, Angelique, and Firestar, with no clear spinoff vector.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in seconds: a flying horse, a sick child, and a mother trying to keep a miracle hidden. That makes the project easy to pitch, easy to market, and easy to cut a trailer around.
strengths.evidence: The opening seahorse image, the winged colt reveal, and the first flight with Angelique on Firestar.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Karissa is a playable lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie gives an actress a contained emotional arc built on skepticism, maternal fear, and late acceptance. That is exactly the kind of role that can attract a respected character actor or prestige-minded lead looking for a warm, accessible showcase.
strengths.evidence: Her resistance to the horse, her conflict over Angelique’s attachment, and her final emotional surrender at the angelic reveal.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The child-and-creature bond is the engine.
strengths.what_it_means: Angelique and Firestar give the film a clean emotional center that can travel across age groups. That bond is the kind of thing family buyers and parents remember, because it turns the fantasy into a relationship story.
strengths.evidence: Angelique naming Firestar, sneaking out to sleep beside him, and riding him in secret.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ranch setting keeps the fantasy grounded.
strengths.what_it_means: The story can be produced as a modest contemporary feature rather than a giant effects movie, which broadens the buyer pool. The stable, fields, house, and local office all support a contained production footprint.
strengths.evidence: Most scenes play on the Boone property, in the barn, or in a handful of nearby interiors.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final angel reveal gives the movie scale.
strengths.what_it_means: The climax opens the story into something mythic, which can elevate the emotional payoff and give the film a memorable ending image. That kind of reveal can help the project stand out in a crowded family-fantasy market.
strengths.evidence: The portal, winged stallions, and Angelique’s transition into the angelic procession.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, pitchable family fantasy with a strong emotional spine: a mother, a dying daughter, and a flying horse that turns grief into wonder. The ranch setting keeps it producible in indie territory, while the creature imagery and angelic climax give it the kind of trailer moments buyers can actually sell.

items.area: The finale pivots hard into celestial fantasy.
items.detail: The last act moves from grounded miracle drama into a full angel-army portal sequence with lightning, armored riders, and a heavenly extraction. That is a meaningful positioning choice for buyers, because it broadens the spectacle but also narrows the audience from simple family drama into overt religious-fantasy territory.

items.area: Angelique is carrying the emotional load.
items.detail: The movie depends on a child performer who can sell illness, wonder, secrecy, and spiritual acceptance without feeling precocious. That is a real casting conversation, because the role is central to the film’s heart and the wrong performance would flatten the whole package.

The horse has to fly convincingly, glow, and interact physically with Angelique in multiple night and daylight sequences. Even in a contemporary setting, that means the project is not a pure contained drama; the VFX and creature work will be a real line item.

items.area: The antagonist arrives late in the game.
items.detail: Martin Thompson doesn’t fully become the threat until well into the story, after the family bond and miracle have already been established. That leaves the back half to carry a lot of external pressure, and the buyer will notice that the human conflict is narrower than the emotional premise.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is tonal and packaging-related: it starts as a heartfelt rural miracle story, then ends as a full celestial intervention movie. The other pressure point is practical — the child lead and the creature effects both have to land for the film to deliver on its own promise.
